newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINLAND BACKS COMMISSION'S EMU STABILITY PACT PLAN.
newsitem.headline: FINLAND BACKS COMMISSION'S EMU STABILITY PACT PLAN.

text.p: Finland supports a post-EMU budget stability pact along the lines of a draft by the European Commission tabled at a European Union finance minister meeting on Monday, the Finnish finance ministry said in a statement.

"Finland accepts the arrangements regarding budget disciplin in the third phase, the so called stability pact, along the lines of the commission's recommendations," the ministry said in a statement received on Tuesday.
The commission's draft plan said that a government found to have an annual deficit above three percent of total output would have to put forward a credible plan to correct it.
"The goal of economic policy must be a balanced public sector economy under normal circumstances," the Finnish finance ministry said.
"Only in this way can economic policy have a favourable impact during later cyclical downturns," Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto said in the statement.

He said it should be up to the council of heads of state and government to rule whether a country's pubic sector deficit in excess of three percent of GDP was due to a so called extraordinary economic downturn.
The commission's draft stability pact discussed at the ECOFIN meeting in Brussels on Monday did not quantify the magnitude of a recession.
"In practice, these kind of matters cannot be defined so exactly that differences in the conditions of member countries could be taken sufficiently well into account in advance," Niinisto said.

Enforcing budgetary rigour within EMU is a prime concern for most of the EU's 15 nations with Germany seen as the staunchest advocate of tight rules. One of Germany's main areas of concern is the lack of a precise definition of a severe economic downturn which would let governments running excessive deficits avoid sanctions.
Juergen Stark, Germany's state secretary for finance, on Monday told journalists that "the timing is not decisive," and argued for an accord that was credible with financial markets and the public.

The tough German stance left Europe's economic powerhouse virtually isolated among the 15-nation bloc, with only the Netherlands showing support for a budget stability pact that incorporates tougher conditions.
